newsitem.title: TURKEY: Government woes send Turkish shares plunging.
newsitem.headline: Government woes send Turkish shares plunging.

text.p: Turkish stocks plunged almost seven percent in Thursday's morning trade over concerns Islamist Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan's coalition may crumble in the face of pressures from the secularist military, brokers said.

The IMKB National-100 closed the morning session 6.85 percent down at 1,427. Turkish financial and capital markets reopened after a 6-1/2-day holiday for the Moslem Eid al-Adha festival and Children's Day.
"The market turned cautious beacuse of increased political concerns. The stock exchange index may fall further today and tomorrow," said Mustafa Arar, general manager of Ari Securities.
Political jitters ahead of a key National Security Council meeting on April 26 and prospects of renewed political uncertainty also gripped money markets.
Bond rates rose by one to four points and the Turkish lira weakened to 134,100 against the dollar from the previous close of 132,600 on April 17.
Press reports that the main oppostion leader Mesut Yilmaz had prepared alternative government models to replace the existing coalition dominated the morning session, brokers said.
Yilmaz, chairman of Motherland Party, offered two different government combinations, grouping several different parties.
Existing party leaders, seen by many as stumbling blocks to past deals, would be excluded from his formulas to take the country to elections in 1998 or 1999, daily Hurriyet reported.

Milliyet newspaper said MPs from both wings of the coalition considered withdrawal or resignation ahead of the meeting of the council which earlier asked the government to implement regulations to combat rising Islamist activism.
The military members of the council are expected to increase pressure on the reluctant government to implement anti-Islamist measures.
Serdar Surer from Ekinciler Securities said political worries, accompanied by a liquidity shortage, would continue to grip the market in the coming days.
The market is short of 71.7 trillion lira ($534 million) on Thursday according to central bank figures.
Some brokers expect stock prices to rebound after the collapse of the government which they believe will pave the way for the establishment of a stronger coalition.
"The index may fall to the 1,350 level by the weekend. But I think the market will be relieved if the government collapses," Korhan Biricik from Deha Securities said.

Arar, of Ari Securities, said any new government to replace the troubled one would be considered as "a solution government" which will take necessary measures to overcome chronic economic and social problems before heading for new elections.
International financial institutions and rating agencies have long been urging Turkey to take urgent measures to correct fiscal imbalances and persistent macroeconomic problems.
The macroeconomic and political instability constrained Turkish banks' ratings, Moody's said in a statement on Wednesday.
Cabinet members earlier said the government was studying a medium-term structural reform package. No details of the programme have been made public.
